lines.watchItem: Merchant-GPU demand is running well ahead of what the chain can ship, with the four largest cloud buyers guiding to about $725 billion of 2026 capital spending and NVIDIA data-center revenue at a record $75.2 billion. Silicon wafer lines are already at full utilisation with spot 300mm prices rising, so leading-edge wafer-start plans sit against a supply base tightening one step further upstream.

Advanced packaging remains booked out, sold out through 2027 at 52 to 78 week lead times with NVIDIA reserving over half of 2026 output, and the reported shortfall still ranges from about 10 percent to about 20 percent. Stacked memory is now the tighter of the two links, with suppliers filling only 60 to 70 percent of requested volume for the next NVIDIA generation, so packaging allocation alone no longer sets realizable accelerator revenue.

The leading-node customer base is shifting toward hyperscaler and model-builder custom silicon: Microsoft is reported to be negotiating capacity for upward of 300,000 Maia 300 chips for 2027 delivery, custom silicon is projected above $25 billion in 2026, and Anthropic is in early talks with Samsung on a 2nm part. At the same time three customers hold more than 85 percent of advanced-packaging output, so a broader customer mix and extreme concentration are running side by side.

Pricing power is sitting with whoever holds scarce capacity: TSMC reported a 67.7 percent gross margin and lifted 2026 growth guidance above 40 percent, NVIDIA held 75 percent, and Samsung raised advanced contract chipmaking quotes 10 to 15 percent on new orders. Memory suppliers are capturing much of the remaining value, with AI rack component costs inflating roughly 2 to 3 percent a week.

Second-source packaging is winning real orders: Google committed to more than 3 million Intel bridge-packaging units for 2028 delivery, Intel Foundry revenue rose 31 percent year over year, and TSMC answered in late July with its own bridge-packaging development. The alternative route carries its own limits, with Intel at roughly 13.7 percent of 2.5D capacity against about 70 percent for TSMC, one fully booked silicon-capacitor supplier, and the technology described as a better fit for custom chips than high-bandwidth accelerators.
